perArtifact.deficiency: It has a solid course structure, but the assessments and schedule are too generic and repetitive to function as a fully teachable syllabus without clearer rubrics, deliverables, and activity detail.
The lesson has accurate core content, but the session arc is overly abstract and templated, with activities that are described generically rather than as concrete classroom tasks.

It covers useful transportation and direction language, but the instruction is still high-level and repetitive, lacking a specific sequence of communicative practice that would make the session feel ready to run as-is.
The guide includes good key terms and checks for understanding, but the retrieval practice is too formulaic and narrow to feel like a robust student study tool without revision.
The course map is plausible but too skeletal: most labs are unnamed generic placeholders, readings are sparse, and the assessments lack concrete descriptions of what students actually do and learn.
The instructional sequence is too vague and repetitive, with activities that do not specify an actual lab task, dataset, or specimen workflow for students to perform.
The concept coverage is solid, but the session activities are still abstract and do not provide a concrete, teachable lab procedure or assessment task.
It is usable and clear, but it is thin: the retrieval practice and concept coverage are too narrow to fully prepare students beyond the most basic distinctions.

The assessment table and schedule are structurally shaky: repeated weekly-response rows, inconsistent close-reading weights, and several sessions with no readings, so it needs real editorial repair before use.
The main weakness is that the plan is overly scripted around a few quoted lines, leaving little room for student-generated interpretation beyond the provided template.
It is strong and teachable, but it leans too heavily on one Eliot passage and one repeated explanatory frame, so the session risks feeling narrower than the outcome set suggests.
The guide is clear and usable, but it is mostly reiteration of the lesson language rather than a broader set of examples or practice that would deepen transfer.

The course description and assessment structure are generic placeholders (studios/portfolio pieces, 14 near-identical image analyses) and do not specify concrete survey readings, artworks, or assignment expectations.
It relies on simplified Greek-vs-Roman binaries and generic image prompts instead of actual named artworks or a fuller range of classical examples, so the content is teachable but thin.
The warm-up/core/practice/closing sections are essentially placeholders and do not spell out the specific artworks, prompts, or comparative tasks students would actually do.
It is compressed into slogan-like definitions and retrieval items, with too little concrete artwork analysis or historical context to prepare students robustly.

The schedule and readings are underdeveloped and inconsistent: most sessions have no assigned text, so the course cannot actually be taught as a reading-based 12-session sequence without adding core primary sources and tightening alignment.

The class activities are too vague and templated to run as-is, especially the core and practice phases, which describe generic engagement with the topic rather than a specific, text-anchored instructional sequence.
The plan is conceptually solid but still too broad and generic, with no concrete primary passage or named reading to anchor the discussion of justice and political philosophy.
It is useful and substantive, but the study prompts remain a bit formulaic and detached from any specific assigned text or argument structure, limiting how precisely students can study from it.
